questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend installing packages into a virtual environment instead of the system Python?
options: A virtual environment isolates a project's packages so installing or upgrading something for one project can't silently break a different project's dependencies
Virtual environments make code run faster than the system Python
pip only works inside a virtual environment and never works on the system Python
Virtual environments are required by law for any scientific computing work
questions.explain: The core risk is that installing directly into the system Python can upgrade or downgrade a package version something else on the machine depends on; a virtual environment keeps each project's installs private.

questions.q: What is the key practical difference between `venv` and `conda` as described in the lesson?
options: conda can also manage non-Python dependencies like compiled BLAS/LAPACK libraries or compilers, while `venv` only manages Python packages and ships with Python itself
venv is a third-party tool that must be separately purchased, while conda is free
conda only works on Linux, while venv only works on Windows
There is no real difference; the two tools are interchangeable in every respect
questions.explain: venv is lightweight and built into Python, handling only Python packages. conda is heavier but can also install non-Python dependencies that some scientific packages need underneath, which is why many research groups standardize on it.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a `requirements.txt` file?
options: It records a project's dependencies, optionally pinned to exact versions, so the same environment can be reproduced later on another machine
It stores the actual source code of all installed packages
It is a Jupyter-specific configuration file with no connection to pip
It replaces the need for a virtual environment entirely
questions.explain: A requirements.txt file is a reproducibility tool: listing exact package versions (via `pip install -r requirements.txt`) lets someone else, or a future you, recreate an identical environment.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say pinning exact versions (e.g. `numpy==2.1.0`) matters more in scientific computing than in typical software projects?
options: A different NumPy minor version can occasionally change default numerical behavior in ways that silently alter a computed result, which is hard to notice in something like a quantum simulation
Unpinned versions always cause immediate crashes, so the risk is identical to any other software
Pinning versions is only relevant for Matplotlib, not NumPy or SciPy
Version pinning has no real benefit and is mentioned only as an aside
questions.explain: The lesson specifically warns that a numerical library's behavior can shift subtly between versions, and that kind of silent change is exactly the sort of bug that's dangerous in scientific/quantum computation, since results can look plausible while being wrong.

questions.q: According to the lesson, which packages does Chapter 1's environment setup install, and which notable category of package is deliberately left out at this stage?
options: NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, and Jupyter are installed; quantum SDKs like Qiskit are deliberately not installed yet
Only Qiskit is installed, since it already bundles NumPy and Matplotlib internally
Only Jupyter is installed; NumPy and SciPy are assumed to be preinstalled on every machine
All major quantum SDKs (Qiskit, Cirq, PennyLane, Braket) are installed immediately in this lesson
questions.explain: The lesson installs the general scientific stack (NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, Jupyter) and explicitly holds off on any quantum SDK, since those come later once the plain-Python/NumPy foundation covered in this chapter is solid.
